eras.x: Law was customary and mostly unwritten, administered by the datu with elders, and varied from community to community. Muslim communities in Mindanao and Sulu followed Islamic law and adat. The “Code of Kalantiaw”, long taught as a pre-colonial code, was shown by the historian William Henry Scott in 1968 to be a 20th-century fabrication; it is not a source of Philippine law.

The Laws of the Indies, the Siete Partidas and royal decrees governed the colony. In the 1880s Spain extended its new codes: the Penal Code (in force here from 1887), the Code of Commerce (1888) and the Civil Code (1889). Much of today’s civil, criminal and commercial law descends from them: the Civil Code’s source notes still cite articles of the 1889 code, and the Code of Commerce remains partly in force.

eras.t: The Revolution and the Malolos Republic
eras.x: The Malolos Congress framed a constitution promulgated in January 1899, establishing a republic with a strong legislature and separation of church and state. It never governed the whole country, but it is the first democratic constitution in Asia and a reference point for later charters.

eras.t: American rule: the Philippine Commission and the Legislature
eras.x: After the Treaty of Paris (1898), the Philippine Commission legislated alone from 1900, then with an elected Philippine Assembly from 1907; the Jones Law of 1916 created a bicameral Philippine Legislature. Their Acts (Nos. 1–4275) introduced American institutions: courts and procedure (1901), the Torrens system of land registration (1902), the Corporation Law (1906), chattel mortgages (1906), the Negotiable Instruments Law (1911), the Administrative Codes (1916, 1917), and the Revised Penal Code (1930), which kept the Spanish code’s structure but rewrote it.

The 1935 Constitution created a presidential system under American sovereignty, leading to independence. The National Assembly’s Commonwealth Acts built the institutions of a state: national defence, the Public Land Act, the first National Internal Revenue Code (1939), naturalization and immigration laws. The Supreme Court’s 1940 Rules of Court replaced much of the old Code of Civil Procedure. The Japanese occupation produced the 1943 Constitution of the Second Republic, which lapsed with liberation.

Independence came on July 4, 1946. Congress enacted Republic Acts that gave the country its own codes: the Judiciary Act of 1948, the Civil Code (1949, in force 1950), the Tariff and Customs Code (1957), the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act (1960) and the Agricultural Land Reform Code (1963). The 1964 Rules of Court governed procedure until the 1997 revision.

eras.t: Martial law and the Batasang Pambansa
eras.x: President Marcos declared martial law in September 1972. The 1973 Constitution, ratified through citizens’ assemblies (its validity was contested in Javellana v. Executive Secretary), was amended in 1976 to let the President legislate by decree. Presidential Decrees codified whole fields: the Labor Code (1974), the Child and Youth Welfare Code (1974), the Insurance Code (1974, recodified 1978), the Property Registration Decree and the Tariff and Customs Code (1978). From 1978 the Batasang Pambansa also legislated: the Judiciary Reorganization Act (1981), the Bouncing Checks Law, the Corporation Code, and the Omnibus Election Code (1985).

After the EDSA People Power Revolution of February 1986, President Corazon Aquino proclaimed a provisional “Freedom Constitution” and exercised legislative power until Congress convened on July 27, 1987. Her Executive Orders of that period have the force of statute; they include the Family Code, the Administrative Code of 1987 and the Milk Code.

The 1987 Constitution, ratified on February 2, 1987, restored a bicameral Congress and expanded judicial review to grave abuse of discretion. Congress has since rebuilt most fields by Republic Act: agrarian reform (1988), the Ombudsman and public-ethics laws (1989), the Local Government Code (1991), the Intellectual Property Code and the Tax Reform Act (1997), the dangerous-drugs, anti-trafficking and anti-VAWC laws, the Revised Corporation Code (2019) and successive tax reforms (TRAIN 2017, CREATE 2021, CREATE MORE 2024). The Supreme Court remade procedure and ethics: the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure (amended 2019), the 2019 Rules on Evidence and the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (2023).

const1987.origin: Each Philippine constitution answered a crisis: independence (1899), self-government under the United States (1935), occupation (1943), authoritarian rule (1973), revolution (1986) and restoration of democracy (1987).
m: 1935 Constitution: presidential system, Commonwealth, then the independent Republic.
Constitution of the Second Republic under Japanese occupation.
1973 Constitution: parliamentary form on paper, amended in 1976 to allow legislation by presidential decree.
const1987.why: The 1987 text reacts against martial law at almost every turn: it limits martial law and requires Congress to review it (Art. VII, Sec. 18), widens judicial review to grave abuse of discretion (Art. VIII, Sec. 1), creates independent constitutional commissions and the Ombudsman, and writes in social justice and human rights.

civil.origin: Before 1950 the Philippines lived under the Spanish Civil Code of 1889. A Code Commission created after independence drafted a new code that kept the Spanish structure and much of its text, added American and other foreign influences, and introduced human-relations provisions (Arts. 19–36).
m: Spanish Civil Code extended to the Philippines.
The Family Code replaces most of Book I on persons and family relations.
Clerical errors in civil registry entries may be corrected administratively (RA 9048).
civil.why: Its articles carry source notes ("(1254a)") that point to the Spanish code they came from: read them to see what was inherited and what was new. The later special laws chiefly modernised family law and civil registration.

family.origin: The Family Code took the family-relations provisions of the Civil Code, reworked them in light of the 1987 Constitution’s equality of spouses and protection of the family, and was enacted by President Aquino while she held legislative power.
m: Executive Order No. 209, the Family Code, signed July 6; amended by EO 227 before taking effect.
Age of majority lowered from 21 to 18 (RA 6809).
Prescription of actions under Art. 36 removed (RA 8533).
Administrative adoption and the National Authority for Child Care (RA 11642).
family.why: Article 36 (psychological incapacity) was the Code’s great innovation and its most litigated provision; see the change of course from Molina to Tan-Andal. Divorce remains unavailable to Filipino couples outside Muslim personal law and Art. 26(2).

rpc.origin: The Revised Penal Code rewrote the Spanish Penal Code of 1870 (in force here from 1887), keeping its classical-school philosophy: free will, crimes graded by stages and participation, and penalties scaled by aggravating and mitigating circumstances.
m: Spanish Penal Code in force in the Philippines.
Death penalty reimposed for heinous crimes (RA 7659).
Rape reclassified as a crime against persons (RA 8353).
Imposition of the death penalty prohibited (RA 9346).
Fines and property values adjusted for inflation (RA 10951).
Age of sexual consent raised to 16 (RA 11648).
rpc.why: Most change has come from special penal laws outside the Code (drugs, graft, trafficking, VAWC, cybercrime), which follow the positivist idea that the act itself is punished, so good faith is no defence (mala prohibita).

labor.origin: The Labor Code consolidated scattered labour laws, from the Eight-Hour Labor Law (1939) and the Industrial Peace Act (1953) onward, into one decree during martial law.
m: Labor Code (PD 442) signed on Labor Day, May 1; in force six months later.
Herrera Law: security of tenure strengthened, reinstatement pending appeal made immediately executory (RA 6715).
Night work of women allowed; the Code to be renumbered (RA 10151).
DOLE publishes the renumbered Labor Code, the edition used here.
labor.why: The 1987 Constitution’s “full protection to labor” (Art. XIII, Sec. 3) and the Court’s doctrines on due process in dismissal (Agabon) and reinstatement (Pioneer, Garcia) shaped how the Code is applied as much as its text.

lgc.origin: The 1987 Constitution promised local autonomy (Art. X). The Local Government Code of 1991 delivered it by devolving services, giving local governments a share of national taxes and creating local special bodies, replacing the Local Government Code of 1983 (BP 337).
m: Local Government Code under the 1973 Constitution (BP 337).
lgc.why: Its fiscal provisions (the internal revenue allotment, now the national tax allotment after the Mandanas ruling) and its disciplinary rules (see the end of the condonation doctrine) are the most litigated parts.

oec.origin: Election law was recodified with each change of regime: the Revised Election Code (1947), the Election Code of 1971, the 1978 Election Code, then the Omnibus Election Code of 1985, which still governs with later amendments.
oec.why: The Code reads as layers: its 1985 core, the Electoral Reforms Law of 1987, synchronized elections (1991), party-list (RA 7941), automation (RA 8436 as amended) and fair elections (RA 9006).

nirc.origin: The internal revenue laws were first codified in 1939, recodified in 1977, and rewritten in 1997. Since then the Code has been amended in large packages rather than replaced.
m: Tax Reform Act of 1997 (RA 8424), in force January 1, 1998.
CREATE: corporate income tax and incentives (RA 11534).
Ease of Paying Taxes (RA 11976) and CREATE MORE (RA 12066).
nirc.why: Because the packages amend sections in place (and RA 9243 and CREATE renumbered some), the section you read is a product of several laws. The app shows each section’s text in force with every amending law beneath it.

rcc.origin: Philippine corporate law began with the Corporation Law of 1906, patterned on American statutes, replaced in 1980 by the Corporation Code, and again in 2019 by the Revised Corporation Code.
m: Revised Corporation Code (RA 11232): perpetual existence, one-person corporations, remote participation.
rcc.why: The 2019 revision aimed at ease of doing business and governance: it allowed one-person corporations, made corporate term perpetual by default, and strengthened the SEC’s enforcement powers.

insurance.origin: The Insurance Act of 1914 gave way to the Insurance Code of 1974, recodified in 1978 and comprehensively amended in 2013.
m: Amended Insurance Code (RA 10607): higher capital, microinsurance, policyholder protection.
insurance.why: The 2013 amendments renumbered much of the Code; cases decided before then cite the old numbers.

nil.origin: The Negotiable Instruments Law of 1911 copied the American Uniform Negotiable Instruments Act of 1896 almost word for word, and is still in force.
nil.why: Because it came from the American uniform act, Philippine courts long treated American decisions on the same text as persuasive. Bouncing checks are punished separately by BP 22 (1979).

pd1529.origin: The Torrens system of title by registration, devised in South Australia in 1858, came with the Land Registration Act of 1902 and was consolidated in the Property Registration Decree of 1978.
pd1529.why: The decree kept the Torrens principles (indefeasible title, the mirror and curtain principles) while consolidating registration of unregistered land and of dealings.

ipcode.origin: Separate laws on patents (1947), trademarks (1947) and copyright (1972) were unified in the Intellectual Property Code of 1997, enacted to comply with the WTO’s TRIPS Agreement.
m: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293), in force January 1, 1998.
ipcode.why: See the treaty registry: TRIPS, Paris, Berne and the Madrid Protocol explain much of its structure.

bp129.origin: The courts created by the Philippine Commission in 1901 were reorganised by the Judiciary Act of 1948 and again by the Judiciary Reorganization Act, which created the Regional Trial Courts and the Metropolitan, Municipal and Municipal Circuit Trial Courts.
bp129.why: Jurisdictional amounts are the provisions that change most: always check which threshold applied when the case was filed.

ra9165.origin: The Dangerous Drugs Act of 1972 was amended many times by decree and statute before it was replaced in 2002 by the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act.
m: Ban on plea bargaining struck down (Estipona v. Lobrigo).
ra9165.why: Section 21 (chain of custody) generated more acquittals than any other provision; RA 10640 responded to that case law.

ra3019.origin: The Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act of 1960 was the first comprehensive anti-corruption statute; plunder (RA 7080, 1991) and the Code of Conduct (RA 6713, 1989) were added after 1986.
m: Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards (RA 6713) and the Ombudsman Act (RA 6770).
ra3019.why: The 1987 Constitution’s accountability article (Art. XI) and the Ombudsman’s powers frame how these laws are enforced.

isl.origin: The Indeterminate Sentence Law of 1933 introduced parole and a minimum-and-maximum sentence, reflecting the positivist aim of rehabilitation within the classical Revised Penal Code.
isl.why: Applying it correctly (the minimum one degree lower, the maximum with modifying circumstances) is among the most tested computations in criminal law.

ra7610.origin: Enacted in 1992 to implement the Convention on the Rights of the Child, which the Philippines ratified in 1990.
m: Special Protection of Children Against Abuse, Exploitation and Discrimination Act (RA 7610).
People v. Tulagan harmonises it with the Revised Penal Code.
ra7610.why: Its overlap with the Revised Penal Code produced the inconsistent rulings that Tulagan tried to settle.

ra9262.origin: Enacted in 2004 to implement CEDAW’s call to address violence against women in intimate relationships.
m: Anti-Violence Against Women and Their Children Act (RA 9262).
ra9262.why: It introduced protection orders (barangay, temporary and permanent) and recognised psychological violence as a crime.

cpra.origin: Lawyers’ ethics began with Canons patterned on the American Bar Association’s 1908 Canons, were codified in the Code of Professional Responsibility of 1988, and were rewritten as the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability in 2023.
m: Code of Professional Responsibility promulgated by the Supreme Court.
Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (A.M. No. 22-09-01-SC), in force May 2023, repealing the 1988 Code and Rule 139-B.
cpra.why: The CPRA added a disciplinary procedure, graded penalties and new duties (online conduct, gender sensitivity, legal aid) that the 1988 Code lacked.

ra6770.origin: The 1987 Constitution created the Office of the Ombudsman (Art. XI); the Ombudsman Act of 1989 defined its powers.
m: Appeals in administrative cases go to the Court of Appeals (Fabian v. Desierto).
Second paragraph of Section 14 struck down (Carpio-Morales v. CA).
ra6770.why: See the changes of course on Ombudsman appeals and on the condonation doctrine.

milk.origin: The Milk Code of 1986 transformed into domestic law the World Health Assembly’s International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes.
m: Pharmaceutical and Health Care Association v. Duque: only the parts transformed into law bind.
milk.why: The leading case on how international soft law does, and does not, become Philippine law.

fire.origin: The Fire Code of 1977 was replaced by the comprehensive Fire Code of 2008.
